passage:
For many years, going to university was considered the best and most reliable path to a good career across Canada. However, as college tuition fees continue to climb and student debt becomes a serious worry, many people are starting to rethink the true value of a traditional four-year degree.

At the same time, a new trend toward "skills-first" learning has become very popular. Instead of spending years studying a wide range of subjects, many students are choosing short trade programs, coding bootcamps, and technical certificates. These focused options let young people learn specific practical skills quickly and start working without massive student loans. Because of this, several major companies have stopped making university degrees a strict rule for job openings, choosing instead to look at a candidate's actual work experience and portfolio.

This shift happens because the job market changes so fast today. Traditional university classes can sometimes move too slowly to keep up with modern technology, leaving some graduates with plenty of theory but little hands-on workplace experience. As a result, a number of recent graduates find themselves taking jobs that do not even require a university education.

On the other hand, many educators point out that university offers much more than just job training. Spending a few years on campus helps young adults learn how to solve problems, think critically, and work well with others. These broader life skills are extremely valuable when industries change and workers need to learn new tasks over the course of their careers. A purely technical training program can make workers great at one specific job today, but a well-rounded education helps them adapt when that job changes tomorrow.

To solve this dilemma, many schools are now trying a mix of both worlds. Some universities offer cooperative education programs where students work part-time in their field while studying, while others let people stack smaller certificates over a lifetime of learning. As the cost of education changes, students are finding creative ways to balance practical job skills with a solid foundation for the future.
